title: Trapped abroad
author: none@none.com (Rabiya Javeri Agha)
content:
FARID left his home in Narowal in search of a better future. A local agent charged him Rs800,000, promising him a well-paid job abroad. What awaited him, however, was nothing he could have imagined. For two years, he says, he was held in a prison-like compound near the Cambodia-Laos border. His passport had been confiscated, his movements were restricted, and his dreams shattered.
Farid’s job was to cook for hundreds of people who, like him, had been trafficked and trapped in scam centres. His working day began at 9am and continued until 4am, leaving him barely a few hours to rest. Any defiance was met with torture, including electric shocks. When authorities launched a crackdown on the scam centre, Farid managed to escape. But his freedom was short-lived as he was apprehended by Cambodian police and remains in a detention centre, waiting to return home.
Despite attempts to seek assistance through Pakistani diplomatic channels, Farid struggled to secure support. He approached the National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) for help, but twice his return was held up by documentation requirements.
Farid’s story is not unique. In May 2026, the government informed the National Assembly of approximately 15,000 Pakistanis reportedly caught up in fraudulent employment schemes or in camps across Southeast Asia. As authorities have begun cracking down on these operations, thousands of Pakistanis now face difficulties returning home. Some need emergency travel documents, while others face penalties and bureaucratic delays. The same parents who struggled to finance their children’s journey abroad are now having to raise more money to bring them home.
We need to look more closely at recruitment networks.
Part of the difficulty is that those who have been trafficked are not always recognised as victims. Young people recruited in one country and forced to commit online fraud in another may themselves face arrest when these operations are raided. Their expired visas or confiscated passports become grounds for detention, while the deception and abuse they have suffered receive far less attention. Worse still, confiscated passports and identity documents may be misused by criminal networks to commit further fraud, potentially implicating victims in crimes they never committed. Even after escaping their traffickers, they stay behind bars, while those who exploited them often remain beyond the reach of the law.
Across its 2025 and 2026 investigations, Amnesty International identified nearly 100 scam compounds in Southeast Asia, documenting human trafficking, forced labour and torture. As authorities have begun raiding these operations, there are worrying signs that similar criminal networks are now taking root in other parts of the world, including Pakistan.
In August 2026, a raid on a suspected illegal call centre in Islamabad resulted in the detention of 500 foreign nationals, including Chinese and Vietnamese citizens. During a visit to Adiala Jail, we met approximately 70 women detained in connection with fraudulent activities.
Were they knowingly involved in fraud, or had some been deceived or coerced into working there? Online fraud is a serious crime and those responsible must be held accountable. But enforcement must distinguish between those who organise and profit from these operations and those who may themselves be victims of exploitation.
Pakistan already has institutions responsible for different aspects of call-centre operations. Yet many of them operate without registration, and there is insufficient monitoring to en­­su­­re that these establishments comply with the law.
A regularly upda­ted registry, coup­led with effective oversight, would help authorities distinguish between le­gitimate businesses and unregistered operations. We also need to look more closely at the recruitment networks operating within Pakistan. Who is offering these jobs? Who receives payment? And what action is taken when families report that someone has been trafficked abroad?
There must be closer coordination between cybercrime investigators, immigration authorities, anti-trafficking agencies and Pakistan’s diplomatic missions. Foreign nationals arrested in suspected scam operations should be screened for possible trafficking and provided with legal assistance. Pakistanis stranded abroad must have access to timely documentation and repatriation, including in countries without a resident embassy.
These are basic responsibilities of a government towards its citizens and towards people who may have been trafficked into its territory.
Farid is still waiting in Cambodia, having survived an experience no one should have to endure. It should not be so difficult to bring him home.
The writer is the chairperson of the National Commission for Human Rights.
Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

title: Pakistan for all
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
WHY haven’t we built a Pakistan where everyone enjoys equal rights? Postcolonial rulers in diverse countries had to build four basic pillars at once: capable states, dynamic economies, cohesive nations, and inclusive politics. Diversity, and in many cases inequalities and conflicts, made the last two vital so that diversity doesn’t mean divides.
But many ignored these subtle tasks to focus on the state and economy, only to make both non-inclusive. This led to conflicts that damaged states and economies. We did the same and faced the same fate. How can we now reverse gears? The answer is simple: ensure inclusive politics to produce a cohesive nation, which can create a capable state that can shape a dynamic economy, with each feeding the others in a virtuous circle. Are we creating this virtuous circle via inclusion or choking it via exclusion?
Inclusive politics needs a political culture where losers can bear losing electorally, knowing they will survive politically to aim for power again. But we have winner-takes-all, zero-sum politics rather than win-win politics — especially in the last four years as the PTI and nationalist parties in KP, Balochistan, and, more recently, Azad Kashmir face not just electoral defeat but also political extinction due to debatable judicial, electoral, and administrative manoeuvres. They are not seen as political rivals to defeat but existential enemies to eliminate. The imposition of emergency rule in KP is the latest such ploy.
Credible elections ensure broad ownership and support for tough decisions. Most of our elections have been controversial. The 2024 elections, in particular, are seen by many credible local and global analysts as having been blatantly rigged. Those elected freely must also be empowered fully once in power. In our case, informal power has long been wielded without accountability. But rarely have elected officials looked as clueless as today. The link between power and accountability to the public stands broken.
Inclusive politics produces a cohesive nation.
While opposing the unconstitutional usurpation of the powers of elected setups, inclusive politics also ensures constitutional checks and balances so that they don’t abuse power. This is done via the horizontal division of power across the executive, parliament, the judiciary, and electoral and accountability state bodies. While such division has always been weak in Pakistan, the boundaries among them have become so blurred in the last four years that the three main power organs look to some like a triumvirate.
Inclusive politics also divides power vertically among federal, provincial, and local setups. Such distribution gives different groups a chance to govern. Those who could not win federally in a given election or can never win there due to their limited support still have a chance to win power provincially or locally. It also brings rulers closer to people to make them more accountable. Concentrating power federally turns too many citizens into permanent losers and reduces accountability. But local bodies elections have not been held for long in most provinces and regions, and provinces have usurped the financial and administrative powers of even those in place. Provinces, in turn, face the same fate at the hands of the centre and some see plans to weaken them further by creating small provinces.
Inclusive politics also empowers individuals and civic groups to criticise elected setups by giving them a wide range of freedoms and rights. But they have been severely curtailed. HRCP’s last annual report des­cri­bes growing curbs on free speech and hu­­man rights. Journa­li­sts, political workers, lawyers, and activists face flimsy cases un­­der draconian cybercrime, sedition, and antiterrorism laws. Threats and disappearances make speaking out dangerous.
Instead of reversing gears, we are actually accelerating on the current self-destructive path. The dream of a Pakistan for everyone has given way to a grim reality of a country for a handful of people who monopolise power and wealth.
Rulers are gaining power but losing legitimacy and trust. Exclusion rather than inclusion, and coercion rather than consent prevail.
The state is struggling to end the violence its past policies helped create, while its current policies risk fuelling violence. A secure state can’t emerge from a divided nation, nor can an economy thrive on exclusion. The inclusionary pillars we neglect will keep weakening the exclusionary pillars we build. With inclusive politics nowhere in sight, a cohesive nation, a capable state and a dynamic economy will remain a pipe dream.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Dengue season
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ANOTHER dengue outbreak looms over the country for reasons of lack of preparedness and negligence. This month’s caseload of the disease continues to surge in KP, with 51 new incidents reported on Sunday. The provincial tally now stands at 4,856. October is the time of year when dengue hits its highest point. According to a report by IDRS at the Directorate General Health Services of KP, as many as 2,244 cases were recorded in the current month. The maximum number of infections was in Kohat: out of a total of 2,822 cases as many as 1,230 form this month’s tally. Not only do these figures lay bare the systemic rot in the health infrastructure, but KP’s virus burden has set the alarm bells ringing in the rest of the country. Last year, the Sindh High Court reprimanded senior health officials for gross incompetence as procurement disputes led to a scarcity of testing kits and it took public fury for fumigation drives to start. Despite cooler weather, Punjab’s hospitals too were inundated with patients. Meanwhile, our underreporting levels are shocking. Most patients either opt for home isolation or go to private clinics and laboratories. This excludes them from official data, rendering the government’s response haphazard and reactive.
In unpredictable climate conditions, official lethargy cannot persist. High humidity and unexpectedly warm temperatures mean a prolonged breeding season for mosquitoes. Moreover, heavy rains and broken drainage only exacerbate the crisis. Additionally, the fact that patients take longer to recover indicates that a more lethal and resistant strain is among us. The authorities must ensure transparent and updated data, prompt management, and most importantly, advance prevention mechanisms. Citizens should not face preventable misery. Cohesive surveillance systems that cover private facilities, testing kits, and adequate knowledge about ever-evolving viral strains are overdue. What was once mild seasonal discomfort has morphed into an all-year public health emergency due to institutional apathy.

title: Privatisation framework
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE proposed merger of the Privatisation Commission and the Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A) into a single institution is a sensible move. It will end the duality of functions and provide a more coherent framework for mobilising private capital to manage public assets and develop physical infrastructure for which the state has limited resources to spare. Although the two bodies operate under separate laws, their mandates intersect in bringing private capital and expertise into areas dominated by the state. A unified entity could offer a common platform for evaluating these options.
Privatisation involves transferring ownership or control of state assets, while public-private partnerships (PPPs) allow governments to enlist private capital for projects they cannot finance. Both approaches require sound financial assessments and clear risk allocations. With Pakistan facing persistent fiscal constraints, the state cannot afford to finance loss-making enterprises indefinitely. Private investment can help ease these pressures, but it is not an end in itself. Poorly structured transactions can leave the state with inadequate returns or costly contractual obligations. The proposed legislation envisages four public funds to support privatisation and PPP transactions. These instruments could help prepare viable projects and attract investment. However, they must not become vehicles for subsidising commercially unsound ventures. Government guarantees and liabilities should be disclosed and assessed before deals are approved. The proposed legal protections for serving and former officials acting in good faith also require careful rethinking. Officials should be protected against frivolous litigation when making decisions in the public interest. Such protection must not, however, become immunity from accountability. Making PPP agreements accessible as public documents is also positive. Public scrutiny is particularly important when private investors enter long-term arrangements that may impose financial obligations on taxpayers and successive governments.
The new arrangement offers an opportunity to improve the management of state assets and infrastructure investment. Its success will depend on securing fair value for public property, attracting credible investors and ensuring that partnerships deliver tangible benefits. The bill proposes a majority-independent board with private-sector representation to strengthen commercial decision-making. Its effectiveness will require transparent appointments, relevant expertise, political independence, clear performance benchmarks, strong accountability, and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules to ensure effective governance. The state must now ensure that commercial discipline, transparency and accountability guide its implementation.

title: AI agenda
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
WHEN asked what he would dress up as for Halloween, a 10-year-old boy I know responded, “Claude, because there’s nothing scarier than AI.” Whether you consider this funny or astute, it highlights the pervasiveness of the AI bogeyman. And the best thing to do with your fears is face them.
So it was good to see Pakistan play a prominent role at the recent Global Digital and AI Summit in Seoul and ramp up engagement with the World Bank to support the country’s digital transformation through a Digital and AI Compact. Pakistan has committed to spending $1 billion on AI by 2030 and is cracking on with plans to digitise 12 key sectors by 2035 under the National Digital Master Plan.
As the momentum builds, we must ask: how will Pakistan fund investment in AI? And what makes digital transformation and AI adoption capable of overcoming structural issues that have held back traditional activities like manufacturing?
AI use — particularly localised AI development and large language model (LLM) training — requires an immense and stable energy supply, high-speed internet and data storage, none of which are readily available in Pakistan. While efforts are underway to boost 5G spectrum and satellite access, the electricity sector is plagued by outages, a dilapidated grid, and circular debt. Concerns abound about whether Pakistan’s scarce water supply can bear the burden of water-guzzling data centres.
Then there’s the question of how to insulate the future of Pakistani youth from widespread AI adoption. Pakistan’s first economic census last year identified that the services sector makes up over 50 per cent of the country’s economy (production is less than 30pc).
How will Pakistan fund investment into AI?
A recent World Bank report notes that the services sector is most vulnerable to AI adoption, with 61pc of Pakistani service workers in jobs with higher-than-average AI exposure. Based on 2024 data, the report indicates that 8pc of all jobs are at risk of being replaced by AI (a number likely to rise). This means many Pakistanis will be trapped in low-skill, low-paying, and climate-vulnerable agricultural or manual labour jobs, while a sliver of society benefits from productivity gains.
The other question is how to prevent the complete securitisation of the AI agenda, a common challenge in countries with national security preoccupations. Concerns about the use of LLMs for mass surveillance have been voiced in the US and China, a scenario that Pakistan, with its punitive electronic crime legislation, is well primed for. Early interest has also been expressed in using AI for smart policing and biometric identity management. An early, advanced data centre was built under a National Aerospace Science and Technology Park initiative. 
The state will feel a growing need to direct AI investment towards national security, because it’s only a matter of time before local terrorist groups begin deploying AI in anti-state activities. Writing in South Asian Voices, Zohaib Altaf and Nimrah Javed highlight the risk of such groups using AI to better target attacks based on intelligence analysis or to support arms development, particularly weaponised drones. The precedent for this has already been set by the Houthis in Yemen, so the likelihood of AI investment being funnelled primarily to military ends is high.
If Pakistan’s AI agenda is not carefully monitored, we face a future in which limited digital infrastructure in the form of resource-intensive data centres is reserved for security-linked AI use, with some private enterprises enjoying gains at the expense of the wider population. In this scenario, urban youth unemployment increases and rural poverty intensifies; agricultural emp­l­o­yment survives the AI rollout, but is ravaged by climate change instead.
There is a way to prevent this scenario. That’s through high levels of transparency and accountability in AI governance, regulation, and investment, including the requirement for public service considerations and consultation as part of all investments. Pakistan’s civil society organisations and media should also redouble efforts to understand the implications of AI investment to ensure accountability.
On a more positive note, the notions of accountability and transparency in AI are no longer antithetical to AI development. US-based civic activism against data centres on resource-use grounds is increasingly effective in blocking projects. And while Big Tech has thrown up its hands, arguing that it can’t be held responsible for what LLMs do, new research suggests that LLMs may be easier to unpick (and so monitor) than we think. Such public-interest considerations, particularly with an inclusion lens, should be part of Pakistan’s AI journey. That may make it less scary. 
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.

title: Encounter culture
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
TEN suspected criminals killed in Karachi police ‘encounters’ in two days should trouble anyone concerned about public safety and the rule of law. Seven died in separate incidents on Thursday and another three on Friday. In each case, police reported armed resistance, exchanges of fire, and the recovery of weapons. These accounts may be accurate, but cannot be accepted without scrutiny. Officers confronting armed criminals have every right to defend themselves and others. Karachi’s residents, long exposed to street crime and violent robberies, deserve protection. Yet the frequency of these so-called encounters raises questions about how operations are conducted and whether suspects are given an opportunity to surrender. Whether the police actions were legitimate or unlawful can only be established through credible investigations. There must be forensic examination of weapons, independent verification of police accounts, and proper documentation of injuries and evidence. Such scrutiny should be routine whenever police gunfire causes death, regardless of the victim’s alleged criminal history. Otherwise, the public must rely entirely on the version offered by those who pulled the trigger.
The concern extends beyond Karachi. In Punjab, where the Crime Control Department faces allegations of staged encounters, the political response has exposed a dangerous willingness to equate police killings with justice. After a suspect in the killing of a teenage worker in Multan died in an alleged encounter, PML-N lawmaker Hina Parvez Butt celebrated it as “justice served immediately”. She deleted the post but defended her remarks as public sentiment. Anger over a child’s murder is understandable. But an elected representative ought to know that public outrage cannot substitute for a trial, and that a police killing is not a judicial verdict. Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari criticised the comments, though the issue is larger than one politician’s embarrassment. Governments must make clear that police performance will be judged by crimes prevented, offenders lawfully arrested, and cases successfully prosecuted, not bodies counted. Independent inquiries into disputed encounters should publish findings and establish responsibility if unlawful force is proved. Police officers need training, equipment and supervision that make arrest a realistic option where possible. A force that can shoot but cannot build a case offers little lasting security. The police are duty-bound to protect lives. They do not have a licence to kill.
Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

title: Season of protests
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
A WAVE of protests is sweeping across the world in a season of unrest. From West to East, the street is confronting the state. Led predominantly by students and young people, protests have been widening to encompass other disaffected groups in society. In some cases, they are morphing into a nationwide movement. On almost every continent, governments are being put on notice that there will be a price to pay for misgovernance and being indifferent to public demands.
    
India’s Gen Z has been in the streets in anti-government protests against the controversial revision of electoral rolls. Students in France began protesting against deteriorating school conditions with other groups, including trade unions, joining demonstrations over high living costs and inequality. In Italy, students, farmers and truckers took to the streets in protests driven by education costs, economic grievances, and anti-war sentiment. In Brussels, students marched over education funding. Spain saw protests over a housing crisis. In Albania, student-led demonstrations occurred over living costs and a controversial tourism project linked to Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. In Portugal, protests erupted over housing and falling living standards. There were education protests across Greece. In Brazil, thousands joined a student march against the election bid of far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Tunisia’s capital witnessed protests demanding the president’s resignation and democratic rights.
The triggers vary, as do the underlying causes. Each protest is rooted in its own political context. But there are common themes. All reject the status quo and indicate disenchantment with traditional political parties. All voice anger against unresponsive governments and the state failing them on their socioeconomic demands.
The context for most protests is a cost-of-living crisis and deterioration or cuts in public services compounded by the state’s inability to deliver on education and jobs. Economic grievances and resentment of inequality are a driving force of the protests. A sense of disenfranchisement is another common thread.
The heavy-handed response by governments to the protests and draconian crackdowns further fuelled the unrest and sparked violent clashes in several places. But it energised demonstrators to keep returning to the street. Unfortunately, in France protests degenerated into looting and rioting.
Protests in Europe and India share a defining feature. They are propelled by a wave of student activism. At their core is youth frustration in a generation that sees broken promises and an uncertain future. It feels betrayed by the lack of educational and economic opportunities. Protes­ters have also been venting rage against political leaders who have ignored public needs and are seen as venal. Initiated by young people, protests have expanded into broader movements as other disaffected groups, with their own set of demands, joined the demonstrations. Social media has been a key mobilisation tool in all the protests.
Governments have been put on notice that misrule and ignoring public needs will have consequences.
None of the protests or movements have been party-led. Political parties have largely been sidelined, even as they tried to leverage the demonstrations; France’s left aligned itself with the protesters. In several European countries, protests are playing out in an environment of deep polarisation, which parties of both the left and right are trying to exploit. This is especially because elections are due next year in many countries including France, Spain, and Italy.
In India, the youth ‘Cockroach’ movement has spearheaded the protests and mounted the most significant challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government so far. The ongoing protests came against the backdrop of student protests led by the Cockroach party over the leak of exam papers in May, which forced the resignation of the education minister. This time, the catalyst was the revision of voter lists by India’s election commission, which apparently involved the removal of around 130 million voters.
The government and the election commission’s claim that this was aimed at eliminating duplicate and ineligible entries was widely rejected. It was instead seen as a step towards mass disenfranchisement. It became the trigger for youth protests, demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner and scrapping the revision. India’s opposition parties also joined the demonstrations and decried the move as a politically motivated purge to benefit the ruling BJP.
The Cockroach Janta Party used the opportunity to broaden its campaign. The government’s strong-arm tactics to suppress the popular upsurge only inflamed the demonstrators who accused Modi of “stealing democracy”. While these protests did not pose an existential threat to Modi, his jittery and increasingly autocratic government behaved as if they did — with arrests and a harsh clampdown. The scale of the protests and the government’s repressive response eroded Modi’s authority, weakened his grip on power, and dented his credibility and image.
    
The mass protests signified much more than opposition to the voter roll overhaul. They have been about democratic rights and democratic ac­­c­o­­untability and against pervasive injustice. As Indian academic Sudhir Kumar Suthar has arg­ued, they have been driven by the quest for dignity as much as for rights. The message from the young is clear: “they deserve a more dignified life than what they have received from the system so far.”
The central question is what will be the outcome of mass protests and what will they achieve? A definitive assessment has to wait until the protests play themselves out as most are still unfolding. But one unintended consequence of the current wave of discontent in some European countries, especially France but to a degree also in Spain and Portugal, may be to strengthen the far-right. The far-right has led none of these protests but it stands to benefit from their fallout.
In a political landscape where the political centre is being hollowed out and centrist parties have lost touch with young people, unrest advantages the most organised opposition force that promises order. In France, that force is Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National. Where the hard-right is in power the advantage works differently. It enables governments to cast the protests as a law-and-order issue fuelled by migrants to justify harsher measures.
More generally, youth-led protests may force governments to take more seriously the needs and aspirations of young people which have rarely been a priority. What the streets are signalling is a breakdown of trust that can no longer be brushed aside. For now, the protests have put governments on notice: misrule has consequences.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

title: Pakistan’s global role
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
THE nature of Pakistan’s role in global politics is once again the subject of much debate. Several officials are ferrying messages between Iran and the US for an end to the conflict, having helped organise a short-lived peace agreement earlier in the year. 
Based on these and past events, there are a series of judgement calls that observers make about the Pakistani state and its position in the world order. One set of views sees Pakistan as a client state of the US, that is, one that’s subservient to America’s imperial interests and its immediate allies in the region, the Gulf monarchies. This view is shared by sections of the left — globally, in the region, and within Pakistan — and disgruntled opponents of the current regime, who furnish as evidence for it the country’s role in global anti-communist politics in the 1950s and 1960s, its partnership with the US against the Soviets in Afghanistan, its role during the ‘war on terror’ between 2001 and 2013, and the proximity of ties with the Trump administration in recent months. Ironically, conservatives and Islamists also cite the 1950s/1960s and the experience of US-Pakistan relations during the war on terror and especially in the last few years, as evidence of successive regimes siding with global secularist interests in subjugating both Islamic movements in the region and Muslim political identity at home.
The other view, held in the same time-space continuum, sees the country as ideologically fundamentalist, and simultaneously, a client of China and an unpredictable ally of the US — one that is capable of undermining the global hegemon on its own or in collaboration with the Chinese. This view is shared by much of the American and Indian mainstream, who cite CPEC and close military relations as an example of Chinese clientelism, previous support to the Taliban during the invasion of Afghanistan as an example of duplicity, and its approach to Kashmir, its recent diplomatic support for Iran, and the broader sociocultural and ideational life of its citizens, as an example of (religious) fundamentalism.
As with most sweeping observations, many may detect a kernel of truth in these otherwise clearly contradictory positions. Close proximity to American imperial interests has characterised many passages in Pakistani political history. Similarly, the relationship with China remains remarkably consistent since the 1970s. However, in an effort to account for Pakistan’s global and regional behaviour, these observations lapse back to the rather broad and imprecise categories of ‘client state’ or ‘fundamentalist state’.
The reality, just on the basis of the actions listed above, is that the state’s geopolitical and ideational positioning has varied considerably, which makes it hard to pin it down as a US ‘client’ of the same ilk as Japan/ South Korea or the Gulf monarchies, or as a Chinese client like North Korea.
There are a series of judgement calls that observers make about the state’s position in the world order.
What is consistent though is the subordinate role that the state here plays in global affairs, not just in terms of geopolitics but also — and more fundamentally — in terms of international economic processes.
How does ‘subordinate’ differ from ‘client’? Beyond mere semantics, a substantive difference is that a subordinate actor may have limited agency, but it retains the capability of understanding and developing its own interests. A client, on the other hand, would, by and large replicate the interests of its patrons.
On the evidence of the last seven decades, it would be incorrect to assert that the Pakistani state elite has not developed a sense of its own interests, even though some may disagree with the content of those interests or how those interests were developed.
There is, for example, a long-standing recognition of being in a ‘tough’ geography, with insecure borders on at least three sides. There is also a persisting notion that it faces a periodically existential threat from a much more powerful eastern neighbour and that this threat should be countered by a military deterrent. This in turn can only be obtained by forging reciprocal relations with more powerful states. 
The presence of these interests/ ideas does not invalidate the fact that the state’s own actions and responses may have hastened insecurities in various ways. Nor can it paper over the fact that the processes through which the state recognises its context and develops its response are heavily skewed towards a largely insulated military-bureaucratic state apparatus. Both, in turn, lead to other domestic problems, including frequent civil-military political conflict and law and order insecurity in the peripheries.
However, while some reduce Pakistan’s subordination to its geography or the original conditions of its creation, one can make the more substantive case that it remains in that place by the nature of the global economic order since the 1970s and due to its own economic dysfunction. 
With basic processes of capital accumulation stagnating or being rendered highly inefficient, the dollar requirement to ensure subsistence-level growth under global conditions of economic liberalisation can only be met through wilful subordination to varied benefactors. Periodic balance-of-payment crises since the 1980s have precipitated this pattern, and geopolitical posturing to extract IMF concessions or rents in other forms has cemented it.
Each successive crisis of the last four decades has found resolution via subordination in the geopolitical domain: favour garnered with the Gulf monarchies via military assistance or labour provision in exchange for reserve deposits; providing the US with regional geopolitical support in exchange for IMF approval, or allowing Chinese capital to make infrastructure investments to kickstart (fleeting) economic growth. Ultimately, each temporary staving off of an economic crisis has pinned down the state’s subordinate position. And in the process little has been done to fix the underlying issue of domestic economic dysfunction. 
The writer teaches politics and sociology.

title: The academic bubble
author: none@none.com (Fatima Waqi Sajjad)
content:
In order to speak about the future one must first recognise the contemporary moment, as it is the contemporary moment that indicates the future — Alexandre Kojève
UNIVERSITIES as places of higher learning have much to say about the future. They talk about AI advancements, new technologies and future skills. Neoliberal universities, however, rarely address the deep-rooted crises of contemporary times. There seems to be a significant disconnect between the everyday realities within a university and those outside it. This is especially troubling in disruptive times like the ones we live in.
I write as a peace scholar who is simultaneously witnessing a critical moment in history and routine academic life inside universities. Global higher education is experiencing deep structural and financial strain. Universities in the UK for example, are facing serious financial turmoil, yet our local universities continue to import their failing neoliberal agendas. Academic institutions in both places seem to have lost touch with the current unsettling realities. 
Many scholars of international relations and peace studies view the current moment as a paradigm-shifting moment in history. We see collapse and chaos all around with brutal genocides in Gaza, Sudan, and Congo, senseless wars in Iran, West Asia, and Ukraine, and illegal interventions in Venezuela and Cuba. Some view the current events as an end to the America-led order, while others view them as the collapse of the post-World War II international rules-based order and the rise of a multipolar or a pluriversal order. Some observers, such as Owen Jones, see a bigger collapse of Western dominance. Some describe the present turmoil as the end of capitalism itself. 
What is happening in our universities as the world falls apart?
An ecological collapse is another reality of the present times. The UN has warned of “a point of no return” as we cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit in the next few years. The death toll from climate disasters continues to rise, with the devastation caused by the glacier collapse in Nepal, the agonising heatwaves in Europe, and the forest fires in Indonesia, Algeria, Canada, and Europe. But all this does not stop capitalist greed, which continues to create a global climate emergency.
So what is happening in our universities as the world falls apart? Lost in the ranking race, they appear inundated with papers, conferences, and funded projects as publication numbers skyrocket, citation scores pile up, and academics are told they cannot pause or they will perish. Hence, the meaning and purpose of knowledge seem to be lost in neoliberal academia. AI adds further layers to the meaningless reproduction of knowledge. Despite an intensifying climate emergency, big tech companies continue to sell visions of AI futures, and universities continue to impose narratives about AI inevitability as if its massive environmental footprint is a secondary issue. We are facing urgent questions about the role of academia in supporting harmful extractive logics that lead to an ecological collapse. There are also serious questions about universities’ complicity in ongoing genocides as evident in the case of student protests for Gaza, which were brutally suppressed by big universities. However, instead of addressing such pressing questions, universities continue to reinforce “the very logic that produced the crises”. 
Urgent and fundamental transformation in our way of thinking is needed. Educational spaces offer hope. They must indulge in greater deliberation to reimagine the future. Decolonial imagination 
has recently gained traction across glo­bal academia and social movements. Decolonial thinking questions modern paradigms of rationality that view knowledge as priv­ate property and re­­search as data extraction. Ins­te­­ad, it explores indigenous knowledge systems based on relationality.
Indigenous cultures have survived on this planet for thousands of years without sophisticated theories of survival and security. They have lived respectfully with the Earth without any technical knowledge of sustainability. The present moment demands that universities pause. They must also halt the ranking race and think about deeper, fundamental questions, such as what is the purpose of knowledge creation? 
Individual success cannot be the purpose of knowledge creation in times of collective failure. The academic fixation with publication metrics is a distraction from the real purpose of knowledge creation, which lies in addressing the grave crises of our times. If universities wish to remain relevant in the future, they must redirect their energies towards building livable futures for all. 
The writer is director, Centre for Critical Peace Studies at the University of Management & Technology & founder of The Pluriversity Lahore.
Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

title: Pakistan export initiative
author: none@none.com (Riaz Riazuddin)
content:
DOES any such initiative exist in our country, or is it a figment of my imagination? For sure, there is an initiative for remittances — but not for exports. One wonders about the presence of one and the strange absence of the other. Exports are stagnating, and remittances are rising. Are exports falling because of unwise policies or despite them? Are remittances rising because of good policy initiatives or despite them? The point here is not to denigrate the remittances initiative or its continually renewed push, but to emphasise that exports should be given greater policy priority than remittances — because, in some growth-promoting way, exports matter far more than remittances. Here we explore the reasons.
This article focuses on increasing exports, not reducing remittances. In fact, remittances should continue to be promoted. Both exports and remittances matter to our economy. Both help contain the current account deficit. Exports are driven by agricultural, industrial, and services output — sectors that already provide a direct impetus to employment in the country. This impetus also has an indirect impact on the economy through spending by household members employed in export industries. Remittances follow increased output in foreign countries that employ Pakistani workers and pay them abroad. Part of their overseas earnings/ savings is sent home to their families. The economic impact of remittances is indirect and arises from spending by remittance-receiving families. Hence, both help fill the gap in the current account, but the growth impact of exports is both direct and indirect, while it is only indirect for remittances.
Another, far more crucial point is that increasing exports to raise the economy’s productivity is paramount for growth. This is not true for rising remittances in Pakistan, although it is theoretically possible if a larger proportion of remittances goes towards export production. Our policymakers seem to have forgotten the importance of exports. A policy to increase exports is more likely to raise productivity than a policy to increase remittances. Increased productivity can fuel long-term sustainable growth. Exporting exposes domestic firms to international competition, better management practices, international quality standards, global supply chains, and new technologies. There is considerable empirical evidence that exporters tend to be more productive and that export expansion can generate productivity gains. For example, the World Bank reports that a 10 per cent increase in exports across its cross-country sample was associated with higher employment, earnings, and productivity.
Another point to note is that exports are always preceded by the actual rise in production and employment (direct impact), as well as the indirect impact through consumption made possible by spending of wages by export-related employees. Contrast this with remittances, whose economic impact is not only indirect but also follows the receipt of remittances. This means that prioritising sustained export growth would create more employment in the country and reduce the desperation of unemployed people pushed abroad to find jobs, even at the risk of their lives. At the same time, increasing exports would have boosted the productivity our economy so badly needs. This is why remittances should not be seen as a substitute for exports. Exports should be promoted with more vigour than remittances.
In terms of promoting growth, exports matter far more than remittances.
Our analysts tend to blame high unemployment almost entirely on high population growth. The fact is that our unwise economic policies are at the root of frequent economic crises that cause growth and productivity to decline. The resulting rise in joblessness leads to greater migration abroad, which, in turn, drives remittances up. Of course, Pakistan’s remittance initiative has helped. But if we had implemented prudent policies that avoided various crises, exports as a proportion of GDP would have risen much faster than remittances.
The export-to-GDP ratio peaked at 17.3pc in 1992 (according to World Bank data). It went down to only 10pc of GDP in 2025. The trajectory of the fall was not linear. Every onslaught of a balance-of-payments crisis precipitated a large decline. It fell to 9.6pc of GDP in 2000 in the wake of the 1998-99 crisis. With more prudent policies after the crisis, it recovered somewhat — only to decline again when imprudent policies followed, leading to other crises between 2000 and now.
In contrast, our remittances have been rising almost consistently during this period as a proportion of GDP. Remittances dipped from 3.2pc of GDP in 1992 to 1.1pc of GDP in 2000, then rose to 9.9pc. The presence of a falling trend in exports and a rising trend in remittances indicates that exports always respond positively to prudent economic policies, while remittances largely show autonomous growth. Refinements in the banking infrastructure have indeed helped to increase remittances, but economic policies also played a role that pushed people into boats to find employment abroad. Subsequent remittance growth has largely occurred despite these economic policies. Pakistan’s export potential is much higher than its current level suggests. The simplest way to estimate what the level of exports could have been in 2026 is to assume the export-to-GDP ratio of 1992 (17.3pc). This translates to exports valued at $78bn, compared with the actual export value of $41bn (FY26 State Bank data).
Frequent balance-of-payments crises in our country seem to have clouded the thinking of our policymakers. When they think about exports or remittances or even foreign investment, they only think in terms of foreign exchange earnings or inflows that fill a gap in the balance-of-payments. Constant firefighting and pressing short- and mid-term foreign financing needs have created a policy psyche that is obsessed with mobilising foreign exchange liquidity and has forgotten productivity and growth. Exports are badly in need of an initiative based on collective policy expertise in the country.
The writer is a former deputy governor of the State Bank of Pakistan.

title: Pak-US reset?
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
SINCE early 2025, Pakistan’s relations with the US have taken an upturn after years of mutual disenchantment. Why did the US opt for this reset? And will this bonhomie last? Historically, Pakistan and the US have come close only when their interests converged. America has preferred a transactional relationship with Pakistan based on specific issues of its geopolitical agenda.
The recent thaw in ties can, therefore, be better understood in terms of how global geopolitics is evolving. It is no longer a unipolar world led by the US. Since the dawn of this century, several centres of power have arisen while the US remains entangled in long, distant wars. The US reliance on its military might to subdue adversaries has taken a heavy toll on America’s world standing.
Into this evolving geometry of global power politics stepped Donald Trump, who has ruptured the trans-Atlantic alliance, pulled back support for Ukraine in its war against Russia, and sought to stabilise America’s ties with China. However, nothing has compromised America’s domestic and international standing more than the recent US-Iran war.
As for Pakistan-US ties, three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw. First is Pakistan’s role in countering terrorism. In March 2025, President Trump thanked Pakistan in his State of the Union address to Congress for apprehending the mastermind of a bombing in Kabul on the eve of the US exit from Afghanistan. Later, Centcom chief Gen Michael Kurilla described Pakistan to Congress as a “phenomenal partner in the world of counterterrorism”. In June 2025, Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief for lunch at the White House. And in August, BLA was designated as a terrorist organisation by the US.
Three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw.
Second, the US, like the rest of the world, saw Pakistan robustly counter Indian aggression in May 2025. The US mediated a ceasefire on May 10. Pakistan acknowledged America’s positive role. New Delhi, on the other hand, was reluctant to acknowledge Trump’s role, even though India itself had asked the US to secure a ceasefire.
Third, Pakistan’s mediatory role in the recent US-Iran conflict has convinced Washington of Pakistan’s important role as a net stability provider in the region.
Meanwhile, America’s distrust of India has deepened because the latter has bought Russian oil while ignoring US sanctions, and has maintained continued economic ties with China while pretending to be a US partner to counterbalance China. America is no longer convinced that India can be a trustworthy counterweight to China.
How will this reset impact Pakistan’s other key relationship? Islamabad’s close ties with Beijing are not unknown to Washington. The Chinese leadership is also well aware of the strategic nature of Sino-Pak relations. In an era where cooperation and confrontation coexist, Pakistan has ample space to pursue mutually beneficial relations with both China and the US based on its own national interest.
India is upset at the uptick in Pakistan’s ties with the US, and its own failure to isolate Pakistan diplomatically. As for Afghanistan, the US has not shown any interest in it, even as the country is on the cusp of becoming a safe haven for world terrorists. The US is also aware of the fine balance that Pakistan has always maintained in its ties with both Iran and Saudi Arabia.
How should Pakistan use this reset in its relationship with the US, even if it was transactional, for mutual benefit? Several promising areas can be identified: Pakistan must ensure that its share of flourishing trade with the US is maintained and enhanced. The US offers bright prospects for Pakistan’s yo­­ung, tech-savvy entrepreneurs, IT exports, startups, software de­­velopment, growing digital adop-
tion, and e-commerce. American companies shou­­ld be encouraged to invest in Pak­istan’s shale oil potential and minerals sector, especially lithium, rare earth elements, and copper — crucial for the semiconductor industry, defence technology and robotics, among others. Other promising areas of cooperation include defence, security, and counterterrorism. Agriculture has been a legacy area of cooperation since the 1950s, as have education and public health. However, all this will only be possible if Pakistan addresses its policy and regulatory hurdles, cost of doing business, security risks, and infrastructure issues.
Today’s Pakistan stands tall as a competent, self-confident power that can contribute to regional peace, stability, and development. However, this window of opportunity may be limited because global geopolitics is constantly evolving. What matters most is making the best use of the recent thaw in Pakistan-US ties while preserving our other key relationships, including with China.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US and is currently serving as chairman of the Sanober Institute.
Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

title: Decoding defence deals
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
SINCE September 2025, Pakistan has signed multilayered and multi-domain defence agreem­e­nts with several Arab and Muslim states. It has sig­­ned a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, the Makkah Joint Def­­ence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, and a defence pact with Kuwait. Pak­istan has recently signed another defence agree­ment — the Badr agreement. Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia are signatories to this pact.
These defence deals have, in the past year, increased Pakistan’s strategic relevance in the Middle East. Interestingly, each accord carries the explicit provision for joint defence production and investment in the defence industry. This clause in every defence pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region. There are four primary strategic factors that have driven Islamabad’s emphasis on the joint defence production clause in each defence pact.
The India factor remains the primary driver. New Delhi’s defence budget now exceeds $80 billion, and its rapid induction of advanced platforms has widened the qualitative gap. Joint production arrangements with middle powers are likely to allow Pakistan to accelerate defence modernisation without bearing the full research and development cost. By manufacturing components and subsystems domestically, Pakistan can sustain a higher operational tempo and maintain credible conventional deterrence.
Islamabad believes that strategic parity in South Asia does not require numerical equivalence. It primarily requires the ability to absorb, adapt, and indigenise technology at a pace that may prevent New Delhi from achieving decisive superiority over Islamabad. These defence deals, therefore, function as a force-multiplier for Pakis­tan’s conventional and strategic capabilities.
Pakistan’s defence pacts over the past year have increased its strategic relevance.
Islamabad’s second strategic objective is the diversification of defence suppliers and reduced reliance of its defence supply chain on Western weapons. Historically, Islamabad has relied on Chinese weapons but the extent of dependency has increased significantly in the last two decades. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute has noted that this dependency is nearly 80 per cent. Although Pakistan and China enjoy unprecedented trust and depth in their all-weather strategic relationship, in theoretical terms, heavy reliance on any single external source worries Islamabad. Similarly, Islamabad is increasingly seeking to decouple its military procurement from Western-reliant supply chains. This approach is rooted in Pakistan’s historically bitter experiences with sudden embargoes and sanctions, alongside Islamabad’s broader resistance to the West’s tendency to use defence exports as political leverage over the Global South during geopolitical crises.
Primarily, Islamabad is eager to cultivate robu­­st, non-Western defence partnerships to secure reliable and uninterrupted arms supplies free from the influence of foreign powers. By integrating affluent Saudi and Qatari capital with the technologically advanced Turkish weapons industry, Pakistan is building an insulated, collaborative defence network with the middle powers to achieve this strategic objective. Islamabad belie­ves that these defence deals, alongside its strategic alliance with China, may allow Islamabad to minimise its conventional vulnerabilities, help mod­­ernise its armed forces, and ultimately achieve a much higher degree of long-term strategic autonomy.
Moreover, Islamabad is acutely aware that the intensifying US-China strategic competition will make it increasingly difficult to maintain a purely China-centric defence supply chain in the long run. Therefore, by building parallel defence production partnerships with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkiye, and Indonesia, Pakistan is creating a middle-power buffer to avoid unwanted political pressure from the US. Interestingly, these countries are not fully aligned with either Washington or Beijing, and provide Islamabad greater room for manoeuvre.
Third, the economic factor equally occupies the strategic motivations of Islamabad. Pakistan wants to enhance its ability to modernise the defence production industry and increase defence exports. Pakistan’s official defence exports stood at approximately $280m in 2024. The recently concluded deals can significantly enhance defence exports to $650-700m by 2027, crossing the $1bn mark by 2030. The Gulf states, seeking to reduce their own dependence on Western suppliers, constitute the most immediate and lucrative market for Pakistani defence exports. Joint ventures under the Badr agreement, MJDA and SMDA are designed to produce systems that meet the Gulf’s operational requirements, while carrying Pakistani certification, and, crucially, a lower price tag. Successful penetration of these markets would generate much-needed foreign exchange for Pakistan, create skilled employment, and justify further capital investment in the domestic defence industry. Beyond the Gulf, there is also potential for niche exports to African and Central Asian countries that face similar budgetary constraints and seek cost-effective, reliable platforms.
The fourth objective linked to the third is to attract foreign direct investment to Pakistan’s defence sector. The joint production clauses are structured to encourage equity participation rather than simple technology licensing. Early commitments already indicate potential inflows of $1.2-1.5bn over the next five years in manufacturing facilities, testing ranges, and human capital development. These investments will upgrade the physical infrastructure of Pakistan’s public-sector defence industry. These inflows can stimulate related industries, including electronics, metallurgy, and software, while creating thousands of high-skill jobs for individuals who would otherwise migrate overseas.
Time will tell whether these defence deals can deliver a meaningful technology transfer. The most important question is whether such a multipronged approach can genuinely enhance Pakis­tan’s long-term strategic autonomy or will merely redistribute its dependencies. It is also unclear to what extent these defence deals can genuinely reduce Pakistan’s strategic vulnerabilities.
However, despite these uncertainties, these defence deals will bring critical capital and technical know-how, while reducing vulnerability to external supply shocks. Yet Islamabad must calibrate its exposure with precision. Over-commitment in the complex security theatres of the Middle East can risk entangling Pakistan in conflicts whose political and military logic lies beyond Islamabad’s core interests. Therefore, Pakistan must pursue these opportunities with strategic clarity and within well-defined red lines.
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: The next Waseem
author: none@none.com (Muna Khan)
content:
I HAVE eight columns left to write this year after this one. I said the last two months should be different. Cheerful maybe. Insightful, at least. Something new. Then Waseem Abbas happened.
He was 15. His father died nine years ago. His mother remarried. A grandfather and an uncle took turns looking after him until they could not. Then they took him to an orphanage in Multan. His grandfather said he wanted the boy to get an education rather than struggle on the streets. That was five years ago.
Waseem wanted to learn electrical work. The orphanage sent him to a contractor, Tauqeer Nazir, after what it says were inquiries. Media reports say Tauqeer had a team of around 40 boys. Six days later, Waseem was dead.
According to the FIR, he ran. He passed residents on a street in a private housing society and told them the men behind him wanted to kill him. A car followed. His head struck a pillar at a gate. His skull was crushed. His cousin says Waseem had often said he did not want to go to the electrician. He wanted to go home. He was buried at 2am in Muzaffargarh. Only close relatives and orphanage officials attended.
Arrest, escape, encounter, closure. We know the sequence well.
Tauqeer was arrested at the scene. Lawyers beat him outside the courtroom, though police were present. A magistrate gave him four days of physical remand. That night, according to the Crime Control Department, he escaped. By the next morning, he was dead, killed in an exchange of fire near Bahawalpur. His accomplice, the CCD says, got away.
Many of us cheered. I understand why. A boy was crushed against a gate, and the man accused of doing it is gone. It feels like the scales have been balanced. But I have read this story before. So have you. Arrest, escape, encounter, closure. We know the sequence well enough to recite it. We know what it says about our policing, and about courts that many people no longer trust to deliver. None of this is a secret.
Last year, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan counted more than 500 alleged encounters in Punjab since January 2025, with over 670 people killed — more than in any other province. It said the killings had become normal since the CCD was set up in February 2025, and that encounters were standing in for the criminal justice system. The CCD rejected the allegations, saying it works within the law and that hardened criminals often fire first.
The statement made the news for a day. Then we moved on. Now some of us applaud. Among them was lawmaker Hina Parvez Butt who tweeted that justice was served immediately. She later deleted it and said it was the feelings of an ordinary citizen. That is precisely the problem. When an elected representative mistakes the killing of a suspect for justice, what hope is there for the ordinary citizen?
So, I have nothing new to say about the encounter, except perhaps this: a trial would have belonged to Waseem. It would have asked questions in public and on the record. Why did a 15-year-old run from the man teaching him a trade? What happened in the six days before? Who is Amjad Ali, the second man named in the FIR, and where is he now? What did the orphanage ask before sending the child away? What happens to the other boys who worked for Tauqeer?
Those questions now have no courtroom. The case against Tauqeer appears to have been closed. The case for Waseem never opened.
Our institutions are often at their most energetic after a funeral. A licence is reviewed — in this case the orphanage’s. A statement is posted. A file is closed, sometimes with a bullet. What we rarely bui­ld is the dull ma­­c­hinery that would have made the fu­­neral unnecessary. A register. An ins­pection. A phone number that a fri­ghtened boy could dial.
Most of us reading this are lucky. When our children turn 15, learning a trade means an internship arranged by a family friend. Someone checks on them. If they hate it, they come home and complain at dinner. Nobody chases them down a street. Waseem had a cousin who listened and a grandfather who hoped. What he did not have was a system.
Somewhere this week another boy is being placed with someone to learn a trade. He may be lucky. The contractor may be kind. But if he is not, and he runs, who will he run to?
I promised myself something hopeful, so here is the most hopeful thing I can find. An old man in Muzaffargarh took his grandson to an orphanage because he believed there was a better life on the other side of its gate. That belief should not be naive.
How many more Waseems before it isn’t?
The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.

title: Prudent warning
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AS speculation grows regarding fresh US-Israeli aggression against Iran, major Muslim states of the wider Middle East, as well as European powers, have clearly expressed their lack of appetite for any such misadventure. Meeting in Istanbul on Friday under the ‘R4+E3’ umbrella, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkiye, the UK, Germany, and France discussed several global hotspots, including Iran and Ukraine. Italy also participated in the meeting. The Turkish foreign minister said that “no one supports” military intervention in Iran at this moment, while France’s top diplomat said any escalation “would only have losers”, besides increasing oil prices, which are already high.
There is good reason for the international community to be worried. Strong signals are emerging from Tel Aviv and Washington that the US and Israel are planning a new assault on Iran, reportedly after the American midterms on Nov 3 — perhaps even earlier. US President Donald Trump has himself said that “we may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the name America gave to the aggression launched in February. While the US leader is known for his bluster and often non-serious threats, in this regard he may actually mean what he has said. The US has been sending more troops and military equipment to the Middle East, and American and Israeli forces have reportedly rehearsed attack plans. Tel Aviv is particularly enthused about going after Iran again.
Doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results each time is equated with folly. But arrogance has blinded both the US and Israel to this reality. Israel had first attacked Iran in October 2024, while both the US and the Zionist state initiated two more aggressive operations against the Islamic Republic, in June 2025 and February 2026. These attacks, particularly the assault launched this year, inflicted huge damage on Iran, decimating its military, political, and religious leadership. But the country regrouped, defended itself, and fought back against the aggressors. The Iranians have reaffirmed that any new attack will be met with “offensive” measures. All of this is cause for alarm. The Gulf states that host American facilities will again be in the line of fire, which is why Muslim countries have warned against a new conflict. But will the war lobbies in Washington and Tel Aviv listen? Many governments and most people of the Middle East are tired of war, and want to rebuild their lives and economies. If conflict and bloodshed return, the shockwaves caused by disrupted energy and trade flows will leave few economies unscathed. Therefore, America should abandon its plans to further destabilise the region. Instead, it should rein in its ally Israel and its bloodthirsty leaders.
Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

title: Russia: pragmatism not appeasement
author: Dr Muhammad Ali Ehsan
content:
With barely a couple of weeks remaining before the US midterm elections, one debate attracting particular attention is President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports and its potential implications for the war in Ukraine. The prevailing interpretation is that Trump is motivated by two immediate objectives: lowering fuel prices to improve his electoral prospects and pressuring President Volodymyr Zelensky to accept his proposed terms for ending the war.

To me, however, this is a simplistic reading of Trump's intentions. I see a broader strategic purpose behind the move, one that extends beyond the immediate electoral cycle and the question of how to end the war in Ukraine. My argument rests on the premise that, given his low approval ratings, Trump may already be anticipating a difficult outcome for the Republicans in the midterms. Rather than focusing exclusively on the election itself, he may be positioning himself for the political landscape that follows it. His longer-term strategy, it seems, is driven by two interrelated ambitions: shaping the legacy he leaves behind as president and improving the Republican Party's prospects in the next presidential election.

The greatest challenge confronting the world today is how to sustain global economic stability and endurance in an increasingly fractured international system. For far too long, the West has portrayed President Vladimir Putin as a dictator leading a dangerous adversary and an autocratic ruler waging a brutal war against a democratic republic. This narrative was consistent with the post-WWII international order constructed by the US and its allies - an order founded on liberal values, a rules-based system and respect for international law. Yet, unnecessary American wars, the retreat of liberal democracy, technological disruption, deglobalisation, mass immigration, deepening political polarisation and the proliferation of grey-zone conflicts have all contributed to the erosion of that order. The actions of Russia and China, therefore, must be understood not merely as challenges to the existing system but also in the wider context of the struggle over what kind of international order will replace it.

President Trump appears determined to secure the distinction of being the American president who brings the war in Ukraine to an end. This ambition, however, may reflect a broader recognition that the international system is changing and that the old order cannot be restored. As illiberal and autocratic tendencies gain ground across the world, the challenge is to develop a new framework of global governance that acknowledges and accommodates the ideological, cultural and civilisational diversity of the international community. Such an arrangement would require the US to make room for both Russia and China within the emerging order, allowing the great powers to compete for influence without being drawn into direct military confrontation. The objective must extend beyond ending the wars in Ukraine and Iran to preventing future conflicts in emerging geopolitical flashpoints, including the Caucasus, the Horn of Africa and the Balkans.

Trump's apparent strategy is to compel Zelensky to the negotiating table by signaling that Washington's willingness to underwrite Ukraine's defence is no longer unconditional. The reported energy ceasefire arrangements, delays in the delivery of American interceptor missiles, restrictions on intelligence-sharing and disruptions affecting Ukrainian drone operations attributed to blocking access to Starlink – all point towards a possible recalibration of American policy. Taken together, these measures could be interpreted as instruments of pressure designed to alter Kyiv's calculations and make a negotiated settlement more likely.

Two historical analogies offer useful insights into what might happen if President Trump succeeds in placing economic pragmatism above the continuation of what I regard as reckless wars in Ukraine and Iran. The first takes us back to the Yalta Conference of February 1945, when Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin discussed the post-war reorganisation of Europe, the future of Germany and the establishment of the UN. Their meeting reflected a recognition that the post-war world could not be organised without an understanding among the great powers. Today, a similar question confronts the international community. Considering that all three are likely to meet first at the sidelines of the Pacific Rim Countries Conference in Hawaii and a month later at the G20 Summit Meeting at President Trump's Doral Resort in Florida, can they find common ground on the principles that should govern an emerging world order? If their anticipated meetings provide an opportunity for meaningful dialogue, the three leaders should use it to develop a workable framework for global governance - one that acknowledges their respective spheres of influence, limits external interference in areas of vital strategic interest and replaces the pursuit of absolute global leadership with an acceptance of great-power coexistence.

The second analogy lies in President Richard Nixon's historic opening to China in the early 1970s. At the time, Washington's rapprochement with Beijing unsettled many American allies, much as Trump's apparent willingness to engage Moscow has generated unease among Western capitals today. Nixon's initiative demonstrated that strategic engagement with an adversary need not amount to surrender; it can instead transform the geopolitical environment and create opportunities that confrontation alone cannot deliver. The US and China had spent years on opposing sides of ideological and geopolitical struggles, yet both eventually recognised the strategic advantages of opening diplomatic channels. The subsequent normalisation of relations culminated in the establishment of formal diplomatic ties in 1979, alongside the US commitment to maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan under the Taiwan Relations Act. If President Trump can persuade Kyiv to participate in a credible peace settlement, the question of guaranteeing Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be central to the negotiations.

The US, Russia and China need to recognise that the pursuit of unconstrained global leadership by any one power can deepen insecurity for all. Their task is to move beyond an endless struggle for primacy. The objective should be a global economy that is vibrant and sustainable and which is capable of enduring geopolitical shocks. If Trump's willingness to engage Moscow can contribute to such an outcome, his legacy may ultimately be measured not by the concessions he made to an adversary, but by whether he helped establish a world in which great powers could compete without continually resorting to war.

title: Breaking the cycle
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE World Bank’s latest Pakistan Development Update sets out what faster reforms could deliver for the economy. If policies and institutions matched those of an average middle-income country, it estimates, annual growth could reach 6.2-6.9pc, enough to reach Vietnam’s current income level, and incomes would triple by 2050. The distance from here is long. Real GDP growth rose to 3.65pc in FY26 and the primary surplus reached 2.9pc of GDP. But per capita income is currently growing at only about 1.6pc, which means the economy has been put in better financial order without making most people better off. The country’s return to macroeconomic stability is widely appreciated by international lenders and credit agencies. However, it is not the same thing as a solid foundation for rapid growth. Much of this stability has come from holding the economy down. High interest rates, fiscal tightening, and costly energy have dampened demand and squeezed imports, easing pressure on the external account. Workers’ remittances have helped the current account and rebuilt reserves, and continued external borrowing has bought time. But none of this builds capacity. Borrowing defers the bill, remittances bring in dollars without adding to domestic output, and compressed imports can fix the external balance while leaving exports no more competitive.
The stability that results depends on inflows continuing and on the government keeping up its restraint. That is why any real push for growth can be risky. It would mean more imported machinery, fuel, industrial inputs, and consumer goods. If exports and productivity do not keep pace, the current account slips, reserves fall, and policymakers enforce tightening again. We have been through this cycle many times. Breaking it means changing what the economy produces and sells, not just how fast it is allowed to grow. The obstacles are well known: unreliable and costly energy, a narrow tax base, cumbersome regulation, weak competition, and a poorly skilled workforce. Policy keeps changing, which deters long-term investment. Tax reform must bring undertaxed sectors into the net, instead of increasing the burden on those already compliant. Energy reform has to cut system costs rather than shift them between consumers and the budget. And exports need a policy that works beyond incentives. Macroeconomic stability cannot carry the economy much further without better productivity.
The World Bank’s numbers are best read as a reform target. Reaching Vietnam’s income level will take sustained spending on education, health, infrastructure, and technology, and institutions that can be trusted. It will also take growth that creates more than just better headline figures. If the government does not use the present breathing space to raise productivity, boost exports, and complete lasting energy and tax reforms, the next growth push could bring back the crisis Pakistan has just come out of.
Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026
